newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak parliament gives govt direct sale power.
newsitem.headline: Slovak parliament gives govt direct sale power.

text.p: The Slovak parliament on Friday approved an amendment to the privatisation law transferring responsibility for direct privatisation of state assets to the government, the official TASR news agency reported.
The state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund (NPF), was formerly responsible for the direct sale of state assets to investors.
The amendment was approved by 75 deputies in the 150-seat parliament, with 26 MPs voting against the legislation while 14 abstained from the vote. Two deputies out of 117 present did not vote.
The new law adjusts privatisation procedures to a Constitutional Court ruling made last November which said the government, and not the NPF, was responsible for direct privatisation.

The Court ruling, however, does not effect retroactively previously approved sell-offs and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar has said the cabinet would not overturn any direct sale decision made by the NPF.
Privatisation has long been one of the hottest political issues in Slovakia, with the opposition repeatedly alleging cronyism, a claim the government denies.
Over the past three years, Slovakia has scrapped mass voucher privatisation and sold off stakes in a number of leading companies without public tenders.
Few details of the sales are ever revealed and the names of the buyers, often linked to company management, rarely mean anything -- even to Slovak market watchers.
Also foreign economic institutions, including the European Bank for Reconstruction and Develpoment (EBRD), have criticised the Slovak privatisation process for its intransparency.

The most controversial sales so far include the two-step privatisation of a majority stake in the country's sole oil refiner Slovnaft a.s. to a management-led group Slovintegra and the sale of a controlling stake in oil and gas storage company Nafta Gbely a.s., both at well under market value.
